Date: 2025-04-15
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (Acme - ML Eng), Lina Gomez (Acme - Platform Lead), Ravi Patel (Acme - Security), Elena (Acme PM)
Recording: Fireflies.ai auto transcript
summary: Redwood SEs reviewed prefix/prompt caching strategy with Acme's ML and platform teams. Main goals: define safe multi-tenant cache keying, estimate expected hit rates, eviction policies, interactions with batching/latency, and security/VPC constraints for a private deployment. Agreement to run a 1k-concurrent request benchmark and share keying design doc. Action items assigned for design doc, prompt sets, and security artifacts.
topics: Quantization and its impact on cache compatibility
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Alright, hey everyone thanks for joining today, um this is the prefix caching strategy review, we're gonna focus on the kv cache, hit rates, keying, multi-tenant safety, and the interaction with batching and quantization.
[00:18] Sam Torres: Yep thanks, uh we ran into some weird bursty patterns in prod so we want to see if prefix caching can shave off token cost and latencies. Our P95 for generation is around 420ms right now.
[00:35] Priya Nair: Cool, and hi everyone, I'm Priya on the Redwood SE side, I'll run through the proposed keying approaches and we can talk tradeoffs.
[00:45] Lina Gomez: Quick note from platform side - we're evaluating Dedicated and Private deployments; security and tenant separation are hard reqs.
[00:55] Ravi Patel: And from security we need KMS integration, audit logs, and proof that cached prefixes don't leak PII across tenants.
[01:05] Alex Kim: Great - we'll call out isolation patterns. Priya do you want to start with the baseline model of prefix caching?
[01:12] Priya Nair: Sure. So the basic idea: cache model KV state for identical prefixes so subsequent generations reuse cached KV cache to avoid recomputing. Keying can be as simple as a hashed prompt string, or we can normalize templates and include context attributes. The tradeoff: more normalization increases hit rate across paraphrases but risks false positives if we over-normalize.
[01:39] Sam Torres: When you say normalized template, do you mean removing entity tokens and replacing with placeholders? We're heavy on user-provided variables.
[01:48] Priya Nair: Exactly. Example: "Write a summary for {{product_name}} features" we'd strip product_name out and include a tenant-id and template id in the key. That keeps per-tenant safety while letting different product instances hit the same cached prefix if semantics match.
[02:02] Jordan Lee: One gotcha: some prompts use dynamic system instructions that change the model behavior nontrivially. If those are part of the template, we must capture their hash or version in the key.
[02:18] Elena (PM): Our PM perspective - hit rates matter but we can't sacrifice correctness. Would prefer conservative keys initially.
[02:26] Priya Nair: Totally, start conservative: include template id, tenant id, and normalized prompt fingerprint. Later you can add paraphrase normalization.
[02:35] Sam Torres: What's the expected hit rate if we do template-based keys? Like rough numbers.
[02:42] Priya Nair: Based on similar customers, with strict template+tenant keys we often see 20-35% hit rates. If you remove tenant or include template-only, that can go up to 45-60% but at the cost of added isolation work and potential leakage.
[02:58] Lina Gomez: 20-35% still sounds useful. For cost modeling can you map that to token savings?
[03:05] Alex Kim: Yes as a back of envelope: if average prompt prefix is 60 tokens and a hit reuses those tokens, each hit saves ~60 decoder tokens compute and associated GPU cycles — so it scales. We'll run numbers in the benchmark.
[03:21] Ravi Patel: How do you guarantee cached state doesn't leak PII? If a prefix includes user-specific content, template normalization won't catch everything.
[03:29] Priya Nair: Two parts: detection + namespace isolation. Detection: flag high-entropy tokens that look like identifiers and either refuse to cache or replace with placeholders. Namespace: always include tenant_id and an ACL in the key, and for multi-tenant hosts we enforce per-tenant logical cache partitions.
[03:46] Sam Torres: So per-tenant logical partitions within the same cache node? We run on dedicated GPU pools but shared cache layer.
[03:53] Priya Nair: Yes, logical partitions keyed by tenant_id plus encryption at rest per tenant if required. For Private customers we can keep cache in a VPC-bound service instance per customer.
[04:05] Jordan Lee: Another approach is key prefixes: e.g., tenant:template:hash. That makes eviction and metrics grouping easier.
[04:14] Lina Gomez: What's the eviction policy recommendation? LRU, TTL, size-based?
[04:20] Priya Nair: We recommend hybrid: per-key TTLs plus an LRU for the working set. TTLs are configurable per template type; high-value templates could have longer TTLs. Also cold-start protection - warm the cache for expected ramp windows.
[04:36] Sam Torres: How does batching interact with hitting the cache? If we batch three requests and one misses, does the model do extra work for all?
[04:44] Priya Nair: Good point. For continuous batching our runtime can partially reuse cached KV for prefixes that match within a batch. If one request misses, we only compute KV for that request; the runtimes merge the KV as tokens are produced. There's some overhead in coordinating multiple KV states but it's much less than full recompute for all.
[05:02] Jordan Lee: Practically, we try to align batching windows by template to improve effective hit rates at the batch level.
[05:10] Sam Torres: Ok, so request coalescing matters.
[05:15] Alex Kim: We should also call out deterministic vs non-deterministic caching. If your prompt uses random seeds or temperature-dependent instructions, caching is less safe.
[05:25] Elena (PM): We do use sampling for some features, so how do you handle that?
[05:30] Priya Nair: Options: cache only up to the deterministic prefix (system + user instruction), then allow stochastic sampling for suffix generation. Another option: canonicalize sampling params into the key; if temperature differs, don't hit.
[05:43] Ravi Patel: From security - we need to log cache reads/writes per tenant for auditability. Is that available?
[05:49] Priya Nair: Yes, Redwood's console exposes per-key telemetry: hits, miss rates, per-tenant breakdown, and audit logs for writes/evictions; those can be shipped to your SIEM.
[05:59] Sam Torres: Can we see per-template hit curves over time?
[06:03] Priya Nair: Yep. We'll include that in the design doc we share.
[06:08] [06:30] Speaker 5: (inaudible) ...
[06:33] Priya Nair: Back to quantization - if you quantize model weights or use a different kernel, does that change cache compatibility? Short answer: yes, cache entries are tied to model variant and quantization profile.
[06:48] Jordan Lee: So we must include model_version and quantization_profile in the cache key metadata.
[06:54] Priya Nair: Exactly. That way, when you roll a quantized variant, cache misses happen and the cache warms for the new variant. For mixed deployments we can fallback: if primary misses, route to compatible model variant with a fallback policy.
[07:08] Lina Gomez: This is important - we plan to run int8 quant on some nodes to save cost. We can't have int8 cached states used against fp16 variant.
[07:16] Priya Nair: Right, incompatible cache entries are disabled by model variant check.
[07:20] Sam Torres: What's the size of a cached prefix (bytes) roughly? If we cache KV, memory could be significant.
[07:28] Alex Kim: It depends on layer sizes and sequence length; ballpark: tens to low hundreds of KB per prefix for large models if you store full KV in float32. Using quantized KV or compressed representations reduces it substantially. Our platform supports quantized KV storage to cut memory by 4x.
[07:46] Sam Torres: So we should plan capacity accordingly.
[07:49] Priya Nair: Yes and note we support TTL-based eviction to bound overall memory.
[07:55] Ravi Patel: For on-prem, do you support customer-managed KMS for cache encryption?
[08:01] Alex Kim: Yes, in Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and keys can be per-tenant.
[08:07] Priya Nair: Also audit logs are kept locally if required.
[08:11] Sam Torres: Are there any risks of stale cached prefixes if templates change?
[08:17] Priya Nair: If template semantics change, you should bump the template version or invalidate cache keys. We recommend automatic template-version hashing as part of the key so redeploys are safe.
[08:28] Jordan Lee: We also provide an API to invalidate by template id, by tenant, or full flush.
[08:34] Elena (PM): Great. On hit rates, you mentioned paraphrase normalization could increase hits - how do you detect paraphrases?
[08:41] Priya Nair: Two paths: lightweight fingerprinting (n-gram + normalized lemmatization) or embedding-based similarity with a small index. Embedding-based gives better recall but higher complexity and risk of false positives - we'd recommend it as an opt-in feature after initial conservative rollout.
[08:59] Sam Torres: Hmm embedding similarity opens safety concerns. We want to avoid mismatches.
[09:04] Priya Nair: Agreed, that's why it's opt-in and we also threshold strictly and require a tenant-level guardrail.
[09:11] [09:30] Alex Kim: Let's talk telemetry and expected metrics we need from Acme for the benchmark.
[09:35] Sam Torres: We'll provide 7 days of production logs, a sample of top 100 templates and their volumes, and expected concurrency profile.
[09:41] Priya Nair: Perfect. We'll run two bench runs: 1) conservative keying (tenant+template+hash) and 2) relaxed (template-only + normalization). We'll measure hit rates, average P50/P95 latency, and tokens saved.
[09:58] Sam Torres: Cool. For bench environment, will this be in our VPC or Redwood's sandbox?
[10:04] Alex Kim: It can be either. For security-sensitive data you can run it in your VPC using our Private evaluation image. If you want speed, we can run in Redwood staging with synthetic anonymized prompts.
[10:17] Ravi Patel: We'll likely want the VPC run for realistic telemetry.
[10:20] Alex Kim: Noted. We'll provide Private eval instructions.
[10:24] Priya Nair: On batching effects - we typically see batching improves QPS but can increase P95 if batch windows are large. Prefix cache reduces per-request compute so you get both latency and cost wins, but tuning batch window / max batch size is critical.
[10:40] Jordan Lee: We recommend adaptive batching: small windows for latency-sensitive routes, larger for high-throughput routes.
[10:46] Sam Torres: How about instrumentation - will Redwood provide per-route token cost breakdown?
[10:50] Alex Kim: Yes, Redwood Console breaks down token cost, cache hit savings, and per-route latency. We'll include sample dashboards in the doc.
[10:59] [11:30] Speaker 5: (crosstalk) ... yeah, and the other thing is uh...
[11:33] Priya Nair: Quick mention on consistency: if you run multiple replicas, cache synchronization uses a consistent hash and either central store or coordinated invalidations. For very low-latency we use local in-memory KV with async background replication.
[11:53] Sam Torres: That async replication could cause short windows of inconsistency - is that acceptable?
[12:00] Priya Nair: For generation prefixes it's ok; but for critical use cases we can use strong consistency mode at cost of higher latency.
[12:09] Lina Gomez: Can we tag templates as "strongly consistent"?
[12:12] Priya Nair: Yes, template metadata supports consistency flags.
[12:16] Elena (PM): On rollback - if you detect a regression after a model or quantization roll, can we atomically fall back to previous model/version?
[12:24] Jordan Lee: Yes, the routing layer supports automatic fallback policies tied to quality SLOs so you can roll back quickly. Eviction of incompatible cache entries is part of the rollout.
[12:34] Sam Torres: For the benchmark please include a scenario with a model variant roll.
[12:38] Priya Nair: Will do.
[12:40] [13:00] Priya Nair: Ok, touching on observability - recommended metrics: per-template hit_rate, hits_per_minute, miss_latency, cache_evictions, memory_usage_by_tenant, and KV_store_io. We'll also emit audit events for reads/writes.
[13:17] Ravi Patel: We need those pushed to our SIEM and for retention to be at least 90 days. Can you support that?
[13:23] Alex Kim: Yes, log forwarding with configurable retention is supported as an add-on.
[13:29] Sam Torres: Any idea on cost delta for enabling long retention and per-tenant encryption?
[13:35] Alex Kim: We'll include options in the pricing doc — encryption + long retention are add-ons in Dedicated/Private SKUs.
[13:41] Elena (PM): Anything else on keying patterns?
[13:45] Priya Nair: One more: include request metadata (api_version, model, template_version, tenant_id) in key canonicalization. Avoid using user-provided fields unless explicitly whitelisted.
[13:58] Sam Torres: Makes sense. For templating system we use internal IDs, we'll provide those.
[14:02] Priya Nair: Great. We'll also propose a safe default blacklist of PII token patterns.
[14:08] [14:30] Alex Kim: Alright let's recap next steps — Priya to share keying design doc, Acme to provide prompt sets and tenant map, run bench in VPC, Redwood to send SOC2/KMS docs and pricing. Follow up meeting 2025-04-22.
[14:50] Sam Torres: Sounds good.
[14:53] Lina Gomez: Thanks everyone.
[14:55] Alex Kim: Thanks, we'll send notes and action items.
[15:00] [END]
